mappings.note: Which object has the higher magnitude of velocity, justified from the steepness of the position-time line. The graph is converted into a kinematic quantity by slope, which is LO-2 rather than LO-1 shape-to-motion reading.

Why uniform circular motion is accelerated at constant speed. LO-1 defines both acceleration and uniform circular motion; this is the 3-mark version of the same demand as O59 and V86, sharing the outcome honestly.

Describe the ring-and-marble activity and what it demonstrates. The demand is to set out a procedure and draw an inference from it, which is the scientific-inquiry competency C8.2; the inference itself is the tangential velocity of LO-1. Splits from V92, which only predicts the outcome (LO-60).

POOR FIT. Define position and reference point and say why a reference point is needed. Nothing in this frame names reference points or relative motion; LO-1 is cited because its definitions presuppose an origin. Recorded with N11, C172, V66 and V67 as one gap.
Difference between average speed and average velocity and why velocity is the fuller description. LO-1 speed/velocity differentiation, with the vector nature as the added justification.
Define uniform and non-uniform motion with everyday examples. LO-1 description of straight-line motion; asked in words, not graphs, which keeps it off LO-2 unlike its S123 cousin.

Free fall: is the acceleration constant, and how is it directed relative to velocity. LO-1 supplies the definition of acceleration, but the gravity content itself is named only at competency level (C2.1) and by no learning outcome.
What the slope of a position-time graph represents and how it differs for fast and slow objects. Both halves name velocity as the quantity taken off the graph, which is the LO-2 operation.

Part (a) identifies the type of motion from the graph shape (LO-1); part (b) obtains displacement from the enclosed area (LO-2). The two parts sit on opposite sides of the shape-versus-quantity split, so both codes are needed.
What average acceleration is and what a negative value indicates. Definition plus sign convention, both inside LO-1; no values given, so it splits from the LO-4 acceleration numericals.
Two parts with different homes: the v=2(pi)R/T formula is C-8.1-LO-2, while zero displacement after one revolution is the LO-1 distance/displacement contrast.

Speed and velocity in uniform circular motion (LO-1), plus why the motion is called an idealised model. That second clause is squarely C8.1, developing appropriate models to represent real-life events, and no other item in the chapter asks about it directly.

What the area under a velocity-time graph represents and how it is computed for motion from rest. LO-2 displacement-from-graph operation; the triangle formula is a reading of the graph, not a kinematic-equation substitution.

Draw a position-time graph for rest followed by constant velocity and explain the horizontal segment. Plotting plus a state-of-motion reading, both in LO-1; nothing is measured off the graph, so LO-2 is out.
Compares distance and displacement on direction dependence and on a return to the start. The scalar/vector half of the LO-1 differentiation clause, stated as a comparison rather than computed.
Merry-go-round: average speed from 2(pi)R/T is C-8.1-LO-2, while the continuously changing velocity is the LO-1 definition of uniform circular motion. Same two-part structure as S115.

Judges a student claim that constant high speed on a straight road means zero acceleration. Tests the definition of acceleration as change of velocity (LO-1); the 100 km/h is decoration, so LO-4 does not apply.
Judges the claim that the magnitude of average velocity can never exceed average speed. LO-1 differentiation clause, justified from displacement being the shortest path; no calculation.

Compares uniform and uniformly accelerated motion by velocity-time graph shape and acceleration value. What is matched is graph shape to type of motion, which is LO-1; no slope or area is evaluated, so not LO-2.

Why a safe following distance is needed, in terms of reaction time and negative acceleration. Exactly identifying the key factors that govern a phenomenon (LO-59), with nothing computed - the qualitative half of the stopping-distance family, opposite N10 and L130.
Trace the steps for getting average velocity from a position-time graph between t1 and t2. The opening clause of LO-2 stated as a procedure; the graph-to-quantity direction rules out LO-1.

All three parts are one outcome: differentiate the quantities, state the equality condition, then apply both to a 3-east-4-north walk. The (c) arithmetic is Pythagoras and s/t, not a kinematic equation, so LO-4 is not added.

Parts (a) and (b) are the definition, SI unit and direction of average acceleration (LO-1); part (c) converts 72 km/h and solves for a and s from the kinematic equations (LO-4). The two halves have distinct homes.

Parts (a) and (b) are the equation set and the constant-acceleration condition that limits it, i.e. properties of the derivation (LO-3); part (c) substitutes 90 km/h and a=-0.5 into v^2=u^2+2as (LO-4).

Three parts, three outcomes: slope and area of a velocity-time graph (LO-2), how the graph shapes for constant velocity and constant acceleration differ (LO-1), and a motorboat displacement computed from u, a and t (LO-4).
